Consolidated, Parent and NAV
Parent versus Consolidated
Parent: only the parent company; from subsidiaries only their approved dividends count as income. The basis for dividends and common in Iranian analysis.
Consolidated: the whole group as one company; intra-group transactions are removed, subsidiaries’ debt and losses aren’t hidden, and “non-controlling interests” are shown separately.

A parent can show high parent profit through profitable sales to a subsidiary or dividends from an indebted child. If consolidated profit is persistently far below the parent’s, the group is weaker than it looks.
Mistake: adding the parent’s profit to the subsidiaries’ profit (double counting).
NAV of Holdings and Investment Companies
Source: the monthly portfolio report on Codal.
Many holdings trade at a discount to NAV; the discount is an opportunity only when management passes it on to shareholders through dividends or asset sales.
NAV = (market value of listed shares + estimated value of unlisted + other assets − liabilities − assumed tax on sale) ÷ number of shares
For years a group’s consolidated profit has been far below its parent profit. Meaning?
The group as a whole is weaker than the parent’s statements show
The group is stronger because profit moved to the parent
No difference; only the parent statements’ profit matters
The parent may be booking dividends from indebted children.
For the whole group’s profit, add the parent’s profit to all the subsidiaries’ profit.
That’s double counting. Use one and explain the difference.
Listed shares 8,000, unlisted 2,000, other assets 500, liabilities 1,500, assumed tax on sale 500 (billion rials), 2,000 million shares. NAV per share (rials)?
NAV per share is 4,250 and the price is 3,000. The discount to NAV, in percent?
When is a discount to NAV an opportunity?
When management passes it on to shareholders through dividends or asset sales
Always; any discount is a guaranteed profit and closes sooner or later, without any trigger
Never; a discount to NAV always stays
Buying a holding only because of its gap to NAV is a common mistake.
Where in Codal do you get a holding’s portfolio data?
The monthly portfolio report
The meeting notice
Investment companies’ monthly reports have a portfolio format.
Explain why a holding’s discount to NAV isn’t always an opportunity.

The discount may last for years. It is an opportunity only when a trigger such as high dividends or an asset sale passes the value on to shareholders. The assumed tax on sale and the quality of management also explain part of the discount.
The discount may stay forever
It reaches shareholders only through a trigger such as dividends or asset sales
Assumed tax and management explain part of the discount
A discount without a trigger is a trap.

A Practical Rule
For each stock write one line: “If the government made one bad decision tomorrow, what would it be and what percent of profit would it take?”
A company whose profit depends on one government decision needs a bigger margin of safety (a shorter payback).

The rate the company can actually get (official/negotiated)
The free-market rate that day, because it is the most real rate

Options, Capital Structure, Article 141
Options
For FIS they aren’t a main tool. A sensible use: a put option as temporary insurance on a stock you own.
Buying call options to speculate, or selling options without understanding margin and leverage = the same risk of ruin.
Embedded put option (taba’i guarantee): a set floor on the loss, but look at the risk of the guaranteeing issuer (please check the details).
Capital Structure and Article 141
Use debt-to-equity in Iran with caution; equity is at historical cost.
Better: bank debt ÷ operating profit (how many years of profit to pay it off) and the effective interest rate against the return on assets.
Article 141: accumulated losses above half the capital → an extraordinary meeting to dissolve or continue. Usually solved by a capital increase from revaluation without fixing the real problem.
A sensible use of options in FIS?
A put option as temporary insurance on a stock you own
Buying call options for quick profit with leverage
Selling options without enough margin for monthly income
Options are a risk-management tool, not the core of FIS.
Bank debt 3,000 and yearly operating profit 1,200. How many years of profit are needed to pay off the debt?
When does Article 141 apply?
When accumulated losses exceed half the capital
When profit exceeds 50% of the capital
When the company pays no dividend
And it is usually solved on the surface by a revaluation.
Solving Article 141 with a capital increase from revaluation fixes the company’s economic problem.
It only moves the capital and loss numbers around; the real problem remains.
Why is the debt-to-equity ratio misleading in Iran?
Equity is at historical cost and below its real value
Bank debt appears only in the notes, not the balance sheet
Retained earnings don’t count as equity
Debt ÷ operating profit is a better measure.
Banks, Insurers and Other Skills

Bank: profit = interest margin + fees − cost of doubtful loans. Property assets and rolled-over loans can hide real losses; auditor qualifications and capital adequacy are decisive. The riskiest group for a beginner.
Insurer: the loss ratio (claims paid ÷ premiums) from the monthly reports, and investment profit on reserves.
Other Valuable Skills
Tax: a legal rate of 25% with exemptions (exports, free zones, listed companies). Take the effective rate and when exemptions end from the tax note (please check the legal articles).
Ownership and free float from tsetmc: a major shareholder who needs cash wants high dividends; a major shareholder who is owed money by the company is a red flag.
Expert revaluation reports on Codal: a free source for the value of land and equipment.
Alternatives: fixed-income funds, gold, index equity funds. If your paper portfolio does worse than a simple fund after 6 to 12 months, that is useful information, not failure.
